 Right Arrow Politics Trump's unusual legal gambit against Biden-era deportation rule pays off at Supreme Court
 The rule allowed immigration judges to delay deportation proceedings while migrants sought asylum or other relief
 By
 Robert Schmad Fox News 
 Published
 October 28, 2026 10:19am EDT Comments

 close Video New York City sanctuary laws upheld as victim's father reacts to court decision 
 New York City sanctuary laws are upheld after a federal judge dismisses a Department of Justice lawsuit, drawing sharp criticism from Joe Abraham, whose daughter Katie was killed in a hit-and-run crash. Meanwhile, New York Gov. Kathy Hochul deflects questions on migrant crime during a gubernatorial debate.

 The Supreme Court, with no noted dissents, has allowed an agreement between Texas and the Department of Justice ending a Biden-era immigration rule to go into effect.
 The Biden administration adopted the rule in 2024, formally establishing procedures for immigration judges to temporarily pause certain deportation proceedings through a practice known as "administrative closure," including when migrants were pursuing immigration relief through other federal proceedings. The Supreme Court's move leaves in place a lower court ruling eliminating that rule, stripping away a procedure that allowed certain deportation cases to be put on hold.
 Texas sued the federal government in June, arguing that the rule was adopted without proper legal authority.
 The Department of Justice agreed with Texas, asking the judge overseeing the case to vacate the rule and prevent similar rules from being adopted in the future.
 JUDGE WHO APOLOGIZED TO ACCUSED WOULD-BE TRUMP ASSASSIN LIGHTS UP DOJ IN HUNTER BIDEN FBI CASE 
 The Texas state flag flies alongside the logo from the U.S. Department of Justice. (Getty Images/DOJ) 
 Opponents accused Texas and the Justice Department of colluding to eliminate the Biden-era rule, arguing that the two sides worked together despite being on opposite sides of the lawsuit.
 On the same day the DOJ made its request, District Judge Reed O’Connor, an appointee of President George W. Bush, granted it.
 TRUMP-APPOINTED JUDGE SLAMS DOOR ON DOJ AS COURT LOSSES PILE UP DAYS AHEAD OF MIDTERMS' 
 Texas Gov. Greg Abbott, a Republican, said his working relationship with President Donald Trump is based on their shared belief in public safety. (Shelby Tauber/Bloomberg via Getty Images; Andrew Harnik/Getty Images) 
 In August, however, three cities with large immigrant populations — Baltimore, Maryland; New Haven, Connecticut; and Columbus, Ohio — joined with Centro Legal de la Raza, an immigrant legal advocacy group, in an effort to intervene in the case and defend the Biden-era rule on appeal.
 The cities argued that eliminating the rule could lead to residents being deported, reducing their tax revenues and giving them legal standing to challenge the agreement. O’Connor rejected that argument.
 MAMDANI BLASTS FEDS FOR WAGING 'CAMPAIGN OF VIOLENCE AND TERROR' AGAINST NYC'S IMMIGRANTS 
 President Donald Trump, first lady Melania Trump and Texas Governor Greg Abbott participate in a roundtable event at the Hill Country Youth Event Center on July 11, 2025, in Kerrville, Texas. (Photo by Chip Somodevilla/Getty Images) 
 On Oct. 9, the three cities and Centro Legal de la Raza asked the Supreme Court to temporarily block the lower court's judgment while their appeal proceeded, accusing Texas and the federal government of engaging in "egregious collusion" to eliminate the Biden-era rule.
 Federal lawyers argued that the cities and their allies lacked legal standing to challenge the agreement because they had not demonstrated the concrete injury required for a federal court to consider their claims.

 "We are deeply disappointed that the Supreme Court declined to intervene to prevent the Trump-Vance administration from dismantling longstanding immigration court procedures through a backdoor agreement with Texas," the cities and Centro Legal de la Raza said in a statement shared with Fox News Digital.
 "For decades, these procedures have allowed immigration judges to temporarily pause deportation proceedings for people pursuing lawful immigration relief, including survivors of violence, abused and neglected children, and victims and witnesses who cooperate with law enforcement," the statement continued. "Eliminating these protections puts vulnerable people at greater risk of deportation and undermines public safety in communities across the country."
